slides.say: Given: a, b and c are integers, c is smaller than b, which is smaller than a, and a plus b is smaller than sixteen. Which of the following cannot be the value of b plus c?

They ask what b plus c cannot be. So we'll find the biggest value b plus c can ever have. [short pause] We'll solve it three ways, by understanding the biggest possible value, by plugging in numbers that make b plus c as big as possible, and by plugging in the answers.
at: They ask what b plus c cannot be

slides.say: [short pause] Let's start with the second given. a and b are integers, so a plus b is an integer too. Smaller than sixteen means at most fifteen.
Now compare the two sums. a plus b is the sum of the two biggest numbers, and b plus c is the sum of the two smallest. Both sums have b, so the difference between them is a minus c.
How big is a minus c? These are integers, so c is at least one below b, and b is at least one below a. So c is at least two below a, and a minus c is at least two.
at: How big is a minus c
c is at least one below b
and b is at least one
So c is at least two below a

slides.say: Start with a plus b, which is at most fifteen. To get b plus c, we replace a with the smaller number c. That takes away a minus c, which is at least two. So b plus c is at most fifteen minus two, which is thirteen. Fourteen is more than thirteen, so b plus c can never be fourteen. Choice number four is our answer.
at: So b plus c is at most fifteen minus two
Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's plug in numbers. We build numbers that make b plus c as big as possible. a has to be bigger than b, and a plus b has to stay at most fifteen. To make b as big as it can be, take a and b as close as possible: a is eight and b is seven. Eight plus seven is fifteen, which is allowed.

c has to be smaller than b, so the biggest c is six. Then b plus c is seven plus six, which is thirteen. If we try a bigger a, like nine, then b can be at most six, and b plus c gets smaller. And b can't be eight or more. Then a is at least nine, and a plus b is at least seventeen. So thirteen is the biggest b plus c can be, and fourteen is out of reach. Choice number four is our answer.
at: so the biggest c is six
And b can't be eight or more

slides.say: [pause] And a third way, plugging in the answers. The question hides a biggest value, so it makes sense to start with the biggest choice, fourteen. Can b plus c be fourteen? c is smaller than b. If b were seven or less, c would be six or less. Then their sum is at most thirteen. So b has to be at least eight. Then a is bigger than b, so a is at least nine, and a plus b is at least seventeen. That's not smaller than sixteen.
at: Can b plus c be fourteen
If b were seven or less
So b has to be at least eight

slides.say: So b plus c can't be fourteen. The question asks for the one value that cannot happen, so we can stop here. Choice number four is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number four is our answer
